\noindent A cell is one combination of campaign, cap, pool, and workload; the curated view aggregates the claim-bearing core-evaluation runs (2{,}092 runs in 260 cells across 14 campaigns), one row per cell, with completions, the modal failure code, median throughput, median 99th-percentile latency, and median peak anonymous memory.
Every campaign row carries a provenance note; campaigns that ran the engine-default 4096-byte buffers describe the unbounded (heap) allocation type regardless of their original intent (Section~\ref{sec:rq3}).

\addchap{Appendix C: Negative-Results Ledger}

Every mechanism or explanation below was tested and did not hold.
Each entry carries its one-line evidence.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Bucket-directory shrink (one-liner):} two-thirds of maps size their directory on uncovered paths; no completion effect.
  \item \textbf{Aggressive / lazy spill thresholds:} no conversion of failing cells in the threshold-sensitivity configuration.
  \item \textbf{Soft threshold derived from the pool:} 0/8 everywhere; cap-derived rule confirmed (8/8 vs 3/8 at the decisive cell).
  \item \textbf{Source admission bound (max\_inflight 64 $\to$ 16):} no change.
  \item \textbf{Task queue bound (1000 $\to$ 8):} no change.
  \item \textbf{Allocation backpressure as a fix:} converted nothing; 10\% throughput cost near the edge; retained as diagnostics only.
  \item \textbf{Levers without pooling (entire first campaign):} mechanically correct, defended an empty pool; conclusion retracted and re-attributed.
\end{itemize}

The data is the 512\,MB \texttt{db\_bench} sweep: 200 configurations (5 write buffer sizes $\times$ 5 block cache sizes $\times$ 4 compression algorithms $\times$ 2 workloads) at 50 repetitions each, 10{,}000 runs, of which 9{,}665 complete.

\subsection*{E.6\quad Backend sizing across the two allocation types: the 16/8 versus 32/32 contrast}
\label{app:rb32}\label{sec:rb32}

% Moved from Chapter 5 (was subsection sec:rb32): the main text holds the backend
% fixed at 16/8; this contrast is additional information on what a larger backend
% would change, outside the evaluation's fixed parameter subset.
This appendix reports, as additional information, what a larger RocksDB backend changes.
The backend runs with a 16\,MB write buffer and an 8\,MB block cache throughout Chapter~\ref{cha:evaluation}.
The microbenchmark behind that choice (Section~\ref{sec:rocksdb-config}) predicted that the larger 32\,MB / 32\,MB configuration, which roughly halves write amplification, should drain fewer bytes and complete more runs once a cap leaves room for it.
A second experiment tests the prediction inside NebulaStream.
It is a single-variable contrast: the write buffer and block cache move together from 16/8 to 32/32, while every other knob, lever, pool size, and workload is held identical.
The hypotheses were pre-registered before the runs: the larger configuration completes more at 1024 and 2048\,MB (H1), completes less at the 512\,MB floor (H2), and does so by writing about a third fewer bytes to the device (H3).
The contrast spans 1{,}938 paired cells.

The result refutes the pre-registration in an informative way.
The effect follows the allocation choice of Section~\ref{sec:rq3}, not the cap alone.
At the tight 512\,MB cap the sign of the effect follows where the window-map pages live (Figure~\ref{fig:rb32-arch}).
Where they live in the buffer pool, the larger configuration helps: the pooled grid W\_ gains 15 percentage points and the pooled lever grid N\_ gains 33 (McNemar $p = 0.002$ and $p < 0.001$).
Where they live on the heap, it hurts: the matched-granularity heap control U\_ loses 38 points ($p < 0.001$).
H2 is therefore refuted for the pooled store it was meant to describe and holds only for the heap configurations, where the larger buffer is pure fixed overhead.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth]{img/fig_rb32_architecture.pdf}
\caption[Backend-size effect on completion, by allocation type]{The backend-size
effect on completion, split by memory configuration, shown at the tight 512\,MB cap. Change in
completion when the RocksDB write buffer and block cache move from 16/8 to
32/32, per campaign, paired by cell. The pooled grids, W\_ (the baseline pooled
allocation) and N\_ (the pooled configuration with pool-pressure levers
enabled), gain; the heap configurations, U\_ (the matched-granularity heap control) and
L\_ (the default-granularity heap configuration), do not. Because both 32/32 configurations ran in
one session and both 16/8 configurations in another, the sign flip is a difference of
differences, so the between-session drift that confounds the absolute numbers
cancels in the contrast. Full per-campaign, per-cap numbers are in the tables of
E.7 below.}
\label{fig:rb32-arch}
\end{figure}

With headroom the larger configuration is a wash.
In the pooled grid it gains 4 points at 1024\,MB and 0 at 2048\,MB, neither significant, so H1 is not supported.
The 512\,MB pooled advantage needs a caveat of its own.
Its two configurations ran eleven days apart in separate sessions, and between-session throughput drift is a known confound (Section~\ref{sec:threats}).
A same-session control re-ran the 512\,MB pooled grid with both configurations interleaved on one freshly formatted card ($n = 80$).
It places 32/32 at 40\% completion against 32\% for 16/8: the same direction as the cross-session figure, but not individually significant (McNemar $p = 0.21$).
The cross-session $+15\%$ is therefore reported as a consistent directional trend, not a significant single-cap effect.

Two findings are robust to the drift.
The allocation sign-flip is a difference of differences, so the session drift cancels in the pooled-versus-heap contrast.
And the memory footprint is stable across sessions: median peak anonymous memory shifts by under one percent while only throughput drifts.
Figure~\ref{fig:rb32-compartments} decomposes that footprint into the pool floor, the unpooled bucket directories, the RocksDB resident set, and the base --- the residual holding everything else resident, the engine and runtime baseline plus the working set the gauges do not attribute (emission and in-flight buffers, slice-store bookkeeping, allocator retention).
The RocksDB compartment is small at every cap; the pool floor and the base dominate the budget, the base being the largest compartment in the completing runs.
A larger write buffer therefore moves completion only at the margin, because it enlarges the smallest compartment.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{img/fig_rb32_compartments.pdf}
\caption[Where the memory budget goes]{Median peak resident anonymous memory of the
pooled grid (W\_) per cap and outcome, as stacked bars over four compartments.
The \emph{pool floor} is the pre-allocated global buffer pool. The
\emph{unpooled directories} are the bucket directories, the per-map
control-block table always unpooled regardless of page size
(Section~\ref{sec:bg-windows}) and allocated as tuple buffers on the heap
rather than in the pool; ChainedHashMap's variable-sized-entry region is
allocated the same way but is never populated by this thesis's fixed-size
UINT64 schema, so it contributes nothing here. The \emph{RocksDB} compartment
is the backend's own resident set; the \emph{base} is the residual, the peak
resident anonymous memory left once the pool floor, the unpooled directories, and
the RocksDB set are subtracted. It is not a fixed floor: it holds the engine and
runtime baseline (resident code, thread stacks, the compiler and query-operator
scaffolding, tens of MB on a release build) together with all resident working
memory the three gauges do not attribute --- the emission pipeline and in-flight
buffers, per-window slice-store bookkeeping, RocksDB working memory beyond its
gauge, and allocator retention --- and it grows with the working set, from 198 to
813\,MB across the three caps (about 40\% of each cap). The RocksDB compartment is
small at every cap; the pool floor and the base dominate, the base being the
single largest compartment in every completing bar. Completing cells carry a
higher resident footprint than the failing ones, which abort before the
working set fills.}
\label{fig:rb32-compartments}
\end{figure}

The mechanism behind H3 did not survive the move from the component benchmark to the system.
On pairs where both configurations complete, 32/32 does not write fewer bytes to the device: it writes more at 512\,MB, the paired comparison at 1024\,MB likewise favors 32/32 writing more, and the two break even at 2048\,MB (tables in E.8 below).
A byte-level gain measured on \texttt{db\_bench} in isolation does not predict the system-level drain under a memory cap.

The analysis is paired throughout.
Each 32/32 cell is matched to its 16/8 twin on cap, pool, state pressure, and configuration, and completion is compared with McNemar's test on the discordant pairs; the unpaired Fisher's test of the pre-registration is underpowered at this pairing.
Cells that die by pool exhaustion or OOM kill are counted as failures, not dropped, so the completion fractions carry no survivorship bias.
The full per-configuration tables follow.

\subsection*{E.7\quad NES-level backend-size contrast: paired completion (32/32 vs.\ 16/8)}
The five tables of E.1 through E.5 characterize RocksDB in isolation.
The contrast below runs the two configurations inside NebulaStream as a single-variable A/B (E.6 above), paired per cell on cap, pool size, state pressure, and configuration.
Completion is the fraction of repetitions that finish; $\Delta$ is the percentage-point change from 16/8 to 32/32; $p$ is McNemar's test on the discordant pairs.
The pooled campaigns (W\_, N\_) gain at the 512\,MB floor; the heap campaigns (U\_, L\_) do not.

\hline
W\_ pooled        & 512  & 80  & 42\% & 28\% & $+15$ & $0.002$ \\
\hline
W\_ pooled        & 1024 & 106 & 41\% & 37\% & $+4$  & $0.541$ \\
\hline

\hline
N\_ pooled levers & 512  & 72  & 99\% & 65\% & $+33$ & $<0.001$ \\
\hline
N\_ pooled levers & 1024 & 96  & 7\%  & 12\% & $-5$  & $0.227$ \\
\hline
U\_ heap (8128)   & 512  & 40  & 18\% & 55\% & $-38$ & $<0.001$ \\
\hline
U\_ heap (8128)   & 1024 & 32  & 44\% & 78\% & $-34$ & $0.003$ \\
\hline

\hline

The 2048\,MB row of N\_ is omitted: no repetition of either configuration completes there.
This table is the data behind Figure~\ref{fig:rb32-arch}.

\subsection*{E.8\quad Drift control and drain mechanism}
Because the two configurations ran in separate sessions, a same-session control re-ran the 512\,MB pooled grid with both configurations interleaved on one freshly formatted card ($n = 80$ each).
It separates session drift from the configuration effect and bounds the absolute 512\,MB claim (E.6 above).

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|l|r|r|r|}
\hline
\textbf{Comparison (512\,MB, $n = 80$)} & \textbf{A ok} & \textbf{B ok} & \textbf{McNemar $p$} \\
\hline
drift: old 16/8 (A) vs.\ fresh 16/8 (B)  & 28\% & 32\% & $0.29$ \\
\hline
in-session: 16/8 (A) vs.\ 32/32 (B)      & 32\% & 40\% & $0.21$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
On cells both configurations complete, the footprint barely drifts between sessions (median peak anonymous memory $-0.3\%$, peak total $0\%$); only throughput drifts ($-49\%$).
Figure~\ref{fig:rb32-insession} shows this drift-free in-session contrast.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.42\textwidth]{img/fig_rb32_insession512.pdf}
\caption[In-session backend-size contrast at 512\,MB]{Drift-free in-session
completion at the 512\,MB cap: 16/8 versus 32/32, both interleaved in one
session on one freshly formatted card ($n = 80$). 32/32 completes 32 of 80
against 26 of 80 (McNemar $p = 0.21$).}
\label{fig:rb32-insession}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:rb32-trace} shows the anonymous-memory trace of one completing run of each backend size.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth]{img/fig_rb32_trace512.pdf}
\caption[Anonymous memory over time, 16/8 versus 32/32]{Anonymous memory over
one completing run of each backend size at a 512\,MB / 16k-pool cell, sampled
every 0.2\,s. Both configurations rise from the same pool-and-base floor near
140\,MB and stay well below the cap; the larger 32/32 write buffer lifts the
peak only slightly. This is the over-time view of the compartment
decomposition in Figure~\ref{fig:rb32-compartments}.}
\label{fig:rb32-trace}
\end{figure}

The pre-registered drain mechanism (H3) is the bytes the backend writes to the device.
On W\_ pairs where both configurations complete, the ratio of median device writes (32/32 to 16/8) is $1.60\times$ at 512\,MB, $0.89\times$ at 1024\,MB, and $1.00\times$ at 2048\,MB, so only the 1024\,MB medians fall below one.
That ratio is sensitive to the aggregation: taken pair by pair, 32/32 writes more at 1024\,MB in 15 of the 18 non-tied pairs (Wilcoxon signed-rank $p < 0.001$), so the per-pair difference runs opposite to the ratio of medians.
No cap shows the byte reduction the component benchmark predicted, and H3 does not transfer to the system.
